“I said, ‘People will say congratulations,’ ” Mr. Walker told Republican activists last month in Columbia, S.C. “ ‘And occasionally there’s going to be someone who reaches out and says they’re praying for you. And that’s not a throwaway line. Nobody says that if they don’t mean it. You need to literally reach out and touch them so you feel the power of that prayer.’ ”
In an email, Mr. Walker recalled that their relationship began to deepen in 2011 when the governor led a fight to strip collective bargaining rights from many public sector unions, which drew tens of thousands of demonstrators and prompted a recall election the next year. (The governor prevailed in both battles.)
“He has been a constant source of support and checked in on me each week (and sometimes daily) during the height of the protests and again during the recall campaign,” Mr. Walker said of Mr. Ryan in an email. “He was particularly interested in whether I was getting enough sleep, time to work out and time for prayer.”
While Mr. Walker does not say Mr. Ryan has supplied specific policy ideas, he echoes, nevertheless, many of the themes Mr. Ryan is now pushing in Congress and championed during the 2012 presidential campaign.
Denouncing “dependency” on the government? Mr. Ryan did so as the vice-presidential nominee; Mr. Walker now says the word with an air of disgust on the campaign trail.
Championing “growth” and “reform”? They have been the organizing principles of Mr. Ryan’s fiscal agenda on the House Budget Committee and as the new chairman of Ways and Means; both are now the economic themes in Mr. Walker’s stump speech. He also urges shifting
Medicaid
money to the states, overhauling
Social Security
before the coming explosion of retirees and changing the federal tax code, issues that for years the governor rarely heard except when he was listening to Mr. Ryan.
“You’ve got to have someone sign something into law, and we don’t have that right now,” Mr. Ryan said at a recent town hall meeting in Mukwonago, not far from where he and Mr. Walker grew up.
By staying on the sidelines in 2016 yet championing conservative tax and spending policies, on which he is widely considered his party’s leading voice, Mr. Ryan could end up playing a role for Mr. Walker and other Republican candidates similar to one Senator Elizabeth Warren may have with Hillary Rodham Clinton on progressive economic issues. He and Ms. Warren are both beloved by their political parties and mocked by those on the other side.
But Mr. Ryan would be extraordinarily well positioned to reshape economic policy under a Republican president. He enjoys good relationships with several of Mr. Walker’s likely competitors. He is especially close to Senator Marco Rubio of Florida (friends say he is enthusiastic about a Walker-Rubio ticket), and is on good terms with Jeb Bush, who named his “
super PAC
” after a phrase — “the right to rise” — that he credited to Mr. Ryan.

Both Mr. Ryan and Mr. Walker are close to the chairman of the Republican National Committee, Reince Priebus, another prominent Wisconsin Republican. But it is Mr. Walker with whom Mr. Ryan has had the longest and deepest bond. They have avoided being rivals so far because they have sped forward on separate career tracks: Wisconsin and state government for Mr. Walker, Congress and national politics for Mr. Ryan.
Mr. Walker was the first to win office, a State Assembly seat in 1993. When Mr. Ryan decided to run for Congress in 1998, Mr. Walker said, he offered to help out if Mr. Ryan’s age became a factor. (It never did.) The two men now share many of the same benefactors, including the billionaire industrialists David H. and Charles G. Koch, and draw ideas from Wisconsin conservative groups like the
Bradley Foundation
.
After Mr. Walker was re-elected governor in 2014, many Wisconsin Republican officials began to worry that he and Mr. Ryan might collide in the 2016 presidential cycle, as it now seems that Mr. Bush and Mr. Rubio, onetime allies from Florida, are likely to do. But there was no late-night strategy session over Miller Lites about which one of them would run. “We never talked about that,” Mr. Walker said.
Rather, Mr. Ryan pulled Mr. Walker aside during an event hosted by the Republican pollster Frank Luntz at a Capitol Hill restaurant, and told the governor that he had decided not to enter the race; Mr. Walker told him and others that he was considering it.
Some Wisconsin Republicans wish Mr. Ryan had not opted out of the race. But others counted themselves lucky to have two Republican powerhouses on the national stage.
Rita Butke, who was Mr. Walker’s shift manager at the McDonald’s here in the 1980s, said she had enthusiastically supported both Mr. Walker and Mr. Ryan because of the values she associated with their low-wage, burger-flipping days.
“There’s a sense of responsibility and humility that you get from a job where you earned only $4.25 an hour,” said Ms. Butke, who is now manager at the Delavan store. “They both learned for themselves how much a dollar meant.”

Richard Lester’s 1968 film, “Petulia,” aimed dead center at the swinging ’60s and hit the bull’s-eye in evoking the disoriented historical moment of the Vietnam War, psychedelia and mod fashion, when everything seemed to be unraveling. To the delirious playfulness of his two Beatles musicals, “Help!” and “A Hard Day’s Night,” Mr. Lester added a new layer of grown-up chaos with this story of a divorced, floundering San Francisco surgeon (George C. Scott); a kooky, free-spirited British beauty (Julie Christie); and her abusive husband (Richard Chamberlain), adapted from a novel by Lawrence B. Marcus. With Nicolas Roeg’s phantasmagoric cinematography and fractured narrative style, which jumps forward and back, this bittersweet movie was way ahead of its time.
“Petulia,” which screens Aug. 10 and 13 at the Walter Reade Theater, is a high point of
Lincoln Center
’s weeklong 15-film retrospective, “Richard Lester: The Running Jumping Pop Cinema Iconoclast,” beginning August 7th, which also includes “The Knack ... and How to Get It,” “Robin and Marian” and “The Three Musketeers.” (

Two leading Republican presidential candidates expressed divergent views on the Voting Rights Act on Thursday, setting up a split within a party that has been accused of seeking to suppress minority voter turnout in the name of combating fraud at the polls.
Asked about the law at a forum in Des Moines, Mr. Bush said he was uncomfortable placing “regulations on top of states as though we’re living in 1960.”
“There’s been dramatic improvement in access to voting,” he said, adding, “I don’t think there’s a role for the federal government in play in most places — there could be some — but in most places where they did have a constructive role in the ′60s.”
He did not detail any changes he might prefer at the state level, but concerning the 1965 federal act, he said he did not support “reauthorizing it as is.”
Most Republican candidates tend to agree with Mr. Bush, but Ben Carson, the retired neurosurgeon who is in second in most polls of Republican voters, did not.
Saying that he wanted the Voting Rights Act to be protected, Mr. Carson told CNN: “Whether we still need it or not, whether we’ve outgrown the need for it, it’s questionable. Maybe we have. Maybe we haven’t. But I wouldn’t jeopardize it.”
Mr. Carson, who is black, went on to say that if he were president, he would reauthorize the act and that he did not understand Mr. Bush’s rationale.
States have had more freedom to change their election laws since the Supreme Court
struck down
a key part of the Voting Rights Act in 2013.
Last year, Senator Rand Paul
appeared to break with his party
on the issue when he said: “Everybody’s gone completely crazy on this voter ID thing. I think it’s wrong for Republicans to go too crazy on this issue because it’s offending people.”
However, he later tempered that sentiment by saying he understood the importance of voter identification requirements.
On Thursday, Democrats accused Mr. Bush of trying to turn back the clock on voting rights.
“Democrats believe that our nation and our democracy are stronger when more people participate, but Republicans continue to try to make voting harder instead of easier,” said Pratt Wiley, the Democratic National Committee’s director of voter protection.
While the issue is a litmus test for Republican candidates, reauthorization of the Voting Rights Act will not come up in the next administration. In 2006, President George W. Bush signed a
25-year extension
to the legislation.
Alan Rappeport reported from New York, and Matt Flegenheimer from Des Moines.
